record.paper_title: An open problem: Why are motif-avoidant attractors so rare in asynchronous Boolean networks?
record.original_question: Which explicit regulatory delays in biological Boolean network models affect long-term dynamics enough to change the biological interpretation of motif-avoidant attractors, and how should modelers decide which edge delays to include when building more realistic asynchronous Boolean models? This includes determining whether a motif-avoidant attractor is an artifact of instantaneous propagation along regulatory edges or a biologically meaningful oscillatory phenotype.

evidence.quote: Increased clarity on the minimal number of delays to eliminate a motif-avoidant attractor will help with the biological interpretation of motif avoidance.

MAAs under asynchronous or random set update retain an element of synchronicity: the effect of a variable’s state change is immediately reflected in all update functions it regulates. Though this may be a useful approximation in many cases, it fails to account for inherent delays in a system, such as when a protein must slowly diffuse through the cytoplasm to reach its target.
Identifying which delays affect the long-term dynamics of a Boolean network would be useful in building more biologically realistic models.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Setting. A Boolean network on n variables is a function F = (f_1,...,f_n): {0,1}^n -> {0,1}^n, where each f_i: {0,1}^n -> {0,1} is the update function for variable x_i. The regulatory (signed) interaction graph G(F) has nodes {1,...,n} and an edge j -> i whenever f_i depends on x_j. Under the (fully) asynchronous update scheme, from a state x in {0,1}^n one transitions to a state x' that differs from x in exactly one coordinate i for which f_i(x) != x_i. The attractors of the asynchronous dynamics are the terminal strongly connected components of the resulting state-transition graph. A trap space is a subcube of {0,1}^n that is forward-closed under every f_i. A motif-avoidant attractor (MAA) is a complex (non-singleton) attractor whose set of states is not contained in any proper minimal trap space of F.

An edge delay is the following local refinement: given an edge j -> i in G(F), one introduces one or more auxiliary "delay" variables y^{(1)},...,y^{(k)} forming a linear chain x_j -> y^{(1)} -> ... -> y^{(k)} -> x_i, replacing the occurrence of x_j in f_i by y^{(k)} and letting each y^{(l+1)} := y^{(l)} (with y^{(1)} := x_j), so that under asynchronous update the signal from x_j reaches f_i only after k independent update events. A choice of delays for F is a function d: E(G(F)) -> Z_{>=0} prescribing the number of delay variables to insert on each edge; let F_d denote the resulting expanded asynchronous Boolean network.

Problem. Develop a principled criterion characterizing which edge delay assignments d alter the long-term asynchronous dynamics of F. Concretely:

(a) Given an asynchronous Boolean network F that possesses a motif-avoidant attractor A, determine the minimum total number sum_e d(e) of edge delays, and the structural location of these delays in G(F), required to eliminate A (i.e., so that F_d has no attractor whose projection onto the original variables coincides with A as a complex attractor not contained in any minimal trap space).

(b) Provide a classification of edges e in G(F) whose delay (d(e) >= 1) can change the existence, identity, or qualitative structure of attractors of F, versus those whose delays leave the long-term asynchronous dynamics invariant.

(c) Using (a) and (b), give a decision procedure for modelers: for an asynchronous Boolean network F arising from a biological regulatory model, prescribe which edges must carry explicit delays so that any MAA of F that persists in F_d may be regarded as a genuine oscillatory phenotype rather than an artifact of the instantaneous propagation assumption inherent in asynchronous update.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in a 2024/2025 work surveying motif-avoidant attractors in asynchronous Boolean networks. Recent results (e.g., empirical large-scale studies and work on linear extensions of edges as delay nodes) show that MAAs are empirically rare and often eliminated by a single linear extension, and partial upper bounds on the number of delays needed to destroy an MAA have been obtained. However, no general characterization of which edge delays affect long-term dynamics, nor a principled criterion for biological modelers, has been established. The problem remains open.

status_evidence.title: An open problem: Why are motif-avoidant attractors so rare in asynchronous Boolean networks?
status_evidence.snippet: Identifies delays / linear extensions as a mechanism that often eliminates MAAs and explicitly poses the question of which delays affect long-term dynamics.
status_evidence.claim: The problem of which edge delays change long-term asynchronous dynamics and the minimal number of delays to eliminate an MAA is stated as open.

status_evidence.title: Strong modules and asynchronous attractors of Boolean networks
status_evidence.snippet: Recent work investigating structural conditions on asynchronous attractors, related to motif avoidance.
status_evidence.claim: Provides partial structural results but does not resolve the general delay question.
